lesson.title: A Nation Built on Slavery: Founding the Confederacy
lesson.summary: In February 1861 delegates from the seceded states met in Montgomery, Alabama to form the Confederate States of America, writing a constitution that explicitly protected slavery and electing Jefferson Davis as provisional president.
lesson.body:
Even before all seven Deep South states had finished formally seceding, their representatives moved quickly to build a new national government rather than simply operate as independent states. Delegates met in Montgomery, Alabama, beginning in early February 1861 and, working with remarkable speed, drafted a provisional constitution within days. On February 9, 1861, the convention elected Jefferson Davis of Mississippi as provisional president and Alexander Stephens of Georgia as vice president; Davis, a West Point graduate, former U.S. senator, and former secretary of war, was inaugurated on February 18, 1861, before a crowd in Montgomery, which briefly served as the Confederacy's first capital.

The Confederate constitution, adopted permanently in March 1861, closely followed the structure of the U.S. Constitution, preserving a similar three-branch government and much of its language. But it made a handful of changes that revealed the new nation's founding purpose. It explicitly protected slavery in any Confederate territory and barred any law denying or impairing the right of property in enslaved people. It also gave more power to individual states, limited the central government's ability to fund internal improvements, and restricted the president to a single six-year term. Alexander Stephens made the new government's priorities unmistakable in a speech delivered in Savannah on March 21, 1861, later remembered as the Cornerstone Speech, in which he described the protection of slavery and the principle of white supremacy as the very foundation the Confederacy was built upon, in direct contrast to the founders of the United States, who he argued had wrongly assumed slavery would eventually die out.

The Confederacy's early leadership faced an immediate practical problem: building a functioning government, treasury, and army almost from scratch while trying to win diplomatic recognition from European powers, especially Britain and France, whose textile industries depended heavily on Southern cotton. Davis and his cabinet hoped that dependence, sometimes summarized as the idea of King Cotton, would force European governments to intervene on the Confederacy's behalf or at least extend formal recognition. That hope never fully materialized, partly because Britain had other cotton sources and partly because British public opinion, once the war became explicitly tied to slavery after the Emancipation Proclamation, made formal alliance with the Confederacy politically difficult.

After Virginia seceded in April 1861 following the attack on Fort Sumter, the Confederate government relocated its capital to Richmond in May 1861, a move that placed the seat of the rebellion only about a hundred miles from Washington, D.C., and shaped much of the war's strategic geography for the next four years. Richmond's proximity to the Union capital made it both an irresistible target for Union armies and a source of constant anxiety for Confederate leaders, who spent much of the war balancing the defense of their capital against the need to fight on multiple fronts across the South.
